output:
*Interview with Rosa Häfeli, maid and cook, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Sit down, Mademoiselle Häfeli. You are not under suspicion. I want the evening in order, one thing at a time. Begin wherever you like.

ROSA: Ja, Monsieur. I was in the kitchen at the back of the house. The champagne glasses for the toast were washed and dried, and I had set them on the tray. Madame wanted them polished twice, and I polished them twice.

MATTHEY: You have a clock in the kitchen.

ROSA: The American one, by the stove. It is a quarter of an hour fast. I keep it so on purpose, so that nothing is ever late. The bread is never late, the soup is never late, and Madame is never kept waiting. I set it myself and I am sure of the quarter hour.

MATTHEY: Tell me about Fräulein Ruedi.

ROSA: Fräulein Lina came down into the kitchen at thirteen minutes to eleven by my kitchen clock, and she stayed with me until after the temple struck eleven. She sat by the table. She did not say much, she never does, but she was very white.

MATTHEY: What did you do while she was there?

ROSA: I worked, Monsieur. I was not going to sit still on the night of the year. There were the glasses, and the bread for the cold plates, and Herrgott, there was so much to do.

MATTHEY: Did you hear anything from the rest of the house while you were together?

ROSA: We heard Madame's piano begin at two minutes to eleven by my kitchen clock. It stopped at eleven minutes past eleven by my kitchen clock. Madame plays Chopin when she is troubled. Everyone in this house knows that.

MATTHEY: You are certain of those readings?

ROSA: As certain as I am of my own two hands. I have told you, the clock is a quarter of an hour fast, and I know it.

MATTHEY: Did you hear the hall clock?

ROSA: I heard the hall clock strike eleven when my kitchen clock showed thirteen minutes past eleven. The old Morbier has its own voice. You hear it through any door in this house.

MATTHEY: Now tell me about going up to the atelier.

ROSA: Madame asked me to fetch the master for the toast. I went up the stairs, past the library, and up the last flight to the atelier. The door was not locked. He was on the floor by his bench. I knelt by him. I called his name, and he did not answer me. Then I went down again, and I did not stop to think.

MATTHEY: Can you tell me the hour when you went up?

ROSA: No, Monsieur. I cannot tell you the hour of that. I only know it was when Madame sent me.

MATTHEY: Did you see anything else in the atelier that you would like to tell me?

ROSA: I saw him, Monsieur, and I saw that he was dead. I did not look at anything else. I was not thinking about the bench or the watches. I was thinking that the glasses were still on the tray downstairs.

MATTHEY: You are frightened of me.

ROSA: Ja, Monsieur. I am frightened of the police. I have never been in a room like this one, with a man writing everything down. In my village the police came only for the stealing of cows.

MATTHEY: I am writing down what you say, and nothing more. You may correct me at any point.

ROSA: Then I will say only what I saw and heard. Madame has been good to me for many years, and I will not say a word against her. I did not see her go up the stairs, and I did not hear her cry. I know she does not cry in front of people.

MATTHEY: Thank you, Mademoiselle. Is there anything you wish to add?

ROSA: Only that my clock is fast, Monsieur, and that it has always been fast, and that nobody in this house was ever late for anything until tonight.
